reference.source: GeneReviews / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses are a group of inherited, mostly autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorders characterised by accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigment (ceroid and lipofuscin) in neurones and other cells
The classical phenotype combines progressive dementia, seizures, myoclonus, motor decline, and (in most childhood forms) visual failure from retinal degeneration
Subtypes are classified by causative gene (CLN1-CLN14) and traditionally by age at onset into infantile, late-infantile, juvenile, and adult forms
Age at onset guides the differential: for example CLN1 often infantile, CLN2 late-infantile, and CLN3 juvenile (Spielmeyer-Vogt) with early visual loss
Ultrastructural inclusion patterns (granular osmiophilic deposits, curvilinear bodies, fingerprint profiles) historically help characterise subtypes
Enzyme replacement therapy is available for CLN2 (TPP1) deficiency, making early recognition of that subtype particularly important
Diagnosis now rests principally on molecular genetics supported by enzyme assays and, where needed, tissue electron microscopy
reference.pathophysiology: The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses are lysosomal disorders in which defects in a range of genes disrupt lysosomal degradation and autophagy. Several subtypes involve deficient soluble lysosomal enzymes (such as palmitoyl-protein thioesterase in CLN1 and tripeptidyl peptidase 1 in CLN2), while others affect transmembrane or membrane-associated proteins of the lysosome and endoplasmic reticulum. Impaired turnover leads to intralysosomal accumulation of autofluorescent ceroid-lipofuscin storage material. Neurones, being long-lived and metabolically demanding, are especially vulnerable, and progressive neuronal loss with retinal degeneration produces the characteristic combination of dementia, epilepsy, motor decline, and blindness.
additionalDifferentials: Other progressive myoclonic epilepsies (Lafora and Unverricht-Lundborg disease)
Other lysosomal storage disorders such as sialidosis and gangliosidoses
Rett syndrome and other regression syndromes in young children
Inherited retinal dystrophy when visual loss predominates early
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic panel testing across CLN genes
Lysosomal enzyme assays including PPT1 (CLN1) and TPP1 (CLN2)
EEG, which may show characteristic changes such as an exaggerated response to low-frequency photic stimulation in some subtypes
Brain MRI to assess cerebral and cerebellar atrophy
Ophthalmological assessment and electroretinography for retinal degeneration, with electron microscopy of tissue where genetics are inconclusive
redFlags: Developmental regression with new seizures and visual failure in a young child
Rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus indicating advancing disease
Bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk in later stages
A treatable CLN2 phenotype that must not be missed given available enzyme replacement therapy
reference.prognosis: Most childhood-onset forms are progressive and life-limiting, leading to dementia, blindness, and loss of motor function, though rate of decline varies by subtype; disease-modifying enzyme replacement can slow progression in CLN2 disease.
pitfalls: Missing treatable CLN2 disease by not measuring TPP1 activity in a late-infantile regression with seizures
Attributing early visual loss to primary eye disease rather than an NCL
Assuming a single uniform disorder rather than a genetically heterogeneous group with different onsets and prognoses
Delaying genetic testing while relying solely on historical electron microscopy
